title: 20 Pitch Deck Edits That Make the Business Easier to Understand
summary: 20 Pitch Deck Edits That Make the Business Easier to Understand
body_markdown:
Most bad decks were designed before anyone decided what they were trying to prove. They have a market slide because decks have market slides and a chart because charts look like evidence. Put a smart reader in front of one, and you find out they can't tell you what the company sells.


Try the following edits on a deck you already have. These are original checks rather than copies of someone else's slides. For useful reference points,[YC's design guide](https://www.ycombinator.com/blog/how-to-design-a-better-pitch-deck/) stresses clarity and readability,[Sequoia's planning guide](https://sequoiacap.com/article/writing-a-business-plan) lays out the underlying questions, and[Pitch's public walkthrough](https://pitch.com/blog/how-we-built-the-pitch-deck-for-our-85m-series-b) illustrates what the process looks like inside one company.


## Make the first three slides intelligible


1. **Make the opening sentence do real work.** Name the buyer, the job and the result. Read it aloud without the company name.
2. **Put one conclusion in the headline.** If two readers could disagree about what they should take away, rewrite the heading.
3. **Use a real task as the problem.** Show the invoice, ticket or handoff that fails. Generic pain makes the product harder to remember.
4. **Show the old way before the new one.** Give both screenshots the same scale and label the elapsed work for each.
5. **State who the product is not for.** A narrow first buyer can make the broader ambition more credible.


## Let the evidence carry its weight


1. **Chart the unit a buyer cares about.** If you are selling a faster close, report time to a reconciled close rather than operations per second.
2. **Give every number a period.** Note whether the evidence is cumulative, monthly or a point-in-time snapshot.
3. **Show the denominator.** Twenty return users means something different in a cohort of 24 than in a cohort of 240.
4. **Label the differences between bookings, revenue and cash.** They can move in different directions. Don't imply they are interchangeable.
5. **Put the source next to the surprising number.** A small appendix reference or unobtrusive source line is enough if the underlying work can be opened.
6. **Mark the forecast as a forecast.** Use a boundary and a different line style. Never let a forecast look like another historical month.
7. **Include a sensible comparison.** If time fell, compare the same work over similar periods and distinguish smaller jobs from faster execution.


## Edit for a distracted reader


1. **Use real labels instead of a color maze.** Put series names beside their lines where they fit. Test the slide in grayscale.
2. **Keep repetition intentional.** Repeat the thesis if the new slide adds proof. Delete a repeated headline with no new information.
3. **Check the smallest screen you will send it to.** Open the PDF on a phone. If a buyer, unit or axis needs zooming, make it larger.
4. **Give cause language a high bar.** A chart can establish what changed. A separate comparison is needed if you want to say why.
5. **Put the strongest objection on the slide or in the appendix.** A bounded answer with a test is better than four arrows pointing up.


## Make the ask and next step legible


1. **Name the next milestone.** A role count is an input. A shorter implementation, higher renewal rate or lower exception count is a result.
2. **Keep the spoken deck and send-ahead deck distinct.** The room can hear transitions. The forwarded PDF has to carry those transitions itself.
3. **Have someone narrate it back.** Ask what the company does, what's been proved and what the money buys. Fix the point where their version falls apart.


## Try it on one slide first


Imagine a chart titled “Fast Growth.” It shows a rising line, but the axis has no units. Replace the title with the actual fact you can defend, such as “Customers using the product weekly rose from 15 to 46 in four months.” Label the weeks, define “using,” and add a note that the figures are illustrative if this is only a mockup. Then ask whether you should show how many people stopped. If the answer changes how a reader understands the business, that belongs in the deck too.


The object of the exercise is not to make a complex business appear simple. It is to leave the complexity where it belongs. The slide can be simple because the work behind it was not.
